messages.subject: Bayes Factor with the brms package (brm function)
messages.subject_clean: Bayes Factor with the brms package (brm function)
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

 

I have been trying to use Bayes Factors(BF)  from the brm function,

and squaring this with the approach of different possible prior shapes
suggested by Dienes (2014, i.e., uniform, normal, half-normal),

 

I was following the tutorial provided by Shravan Vasishth and colleagues in
JPhon

(https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wocn.2018.07.008), and I am getting some results
I do not understand.

 

As proposed in the tutorial paper, to get a BF, I had a model with and one
without an effect.

The effect was a comparison of onset overlap versus rhyme competitors in an
eye-tracking task,
and the dependent measure was target over competitor preference in logit
units.

 

However, since I had an idea of how large the effect should be, I used two
models with an effect.

One with a relatively unspecific prior, a normal distribution of m = 0, sd =
1.5,

meaning that effect larger than absolute 3 logit units are unlikely (which
makes sense for eye-tracking
in a relatively early window).

 

The other model used a more specific prior.

I looked at similar experiments where the average preference for situations
with onset versus rhyme competitors
was about 1.5 logit units (in a 200-600ms window).  Hence, I specified a
prior with a mean of 1.5 and a 
sd of 0.75 (half of the mean, as suggested by Dienes, 2014).

 

Since there was a small preference for the onset competitors, I expected the
first model to give me an undecisive BF,
but the later a clear one, meaning that the effect is definitely closer to
zero than to the typical effect in this kind of design.

To my surprise, I got the opposite. For the unspecific prior (m = 0, sd,
1.5), the BFs were around 0.09 (I tested the stability,
by running the bayes_factor function 10 times), but with the more specific
model (m = 1.5, sd = 0,75) the BF was around 0.25.

In any case, I had expected the BF to support the null more clearly with a
specific prior.

 

This did not makes sense to me, so I went with the observed effect and its
standard error from LMER to the Bayes Calculator

on Zoltan Dienes Webpage. There, I indeed get the expected result that the
BF is smaller (i.e., more decisive) with the more 
restrictive prior. (I know that that probably is not a valid procedure, I
just wanted to test my intuition here.)

 

Any thoughts on what is causing this, and how to use more informed priors
with brm

(the tutorial paper only uses priors with means around zero).

 

Kind regards,

Holger

 

PS: Happy to share data and scripts, also have the Bayesian models saved,
but they do not fit through email (surprisingly: 0.6GB)
